questions.title: How does the Federal Circuit's substantial evidence standard interact with the regional circuit's JMOL standard?
questions.question_body: I'm reading Finesse Wireless v. AT&T Mobility, and the court says it reviews JMOL denials under regional circuit law (Fifth Circuit here) but also reviews jury findings for 'substantial evidence.' The Fifth Circuit standard asks whether 'reasonable jurors could not arrive at any contrary conclusion,' while substantial evidence asks whether 'a reasonable jury could have found in favor of the prevailing party.' These sound like opposite directions of the same question. Are they actually different standards, or are they just two ways of asking the same thing? How do courts apply both in practice?

questions.title: When does contradictory expert testimony become insufficient to support a jury verdict?
questions.question_body: In Finesse Wireless, the expert Dr. Wells kept testifying that the 'modeled PIM path' was the 'interference generating signals,' but on cross-examination he seemed to pivot and say something about x1 and x2 signals instead. The Federal Circuit cited Johns Hopkins v. Datascope Corp. and held this 'confusing change of course' wasn't sufficient evidence. But isn't weighing conflicting testimony exactly what juries are supposed to do? At what point does contradictory expert testimony cross the line from 'credibility issue for the jury' to 'legally insufficient evidence'?

questions.title: What is the difference between 'separately identifiable' and 'unique' signals in patent claim construction?
questions.question_body: The district court in Finesse Wireless construed 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' to mean 'separately identifiable' but not 'unique' signals. The court said using two signals plus a copy of one could meet this construction. But doesn't 'separately identifiable' mean they have to be different from each other? If I have signal S1 and then make a copy of it, aren't those two things just the same signal twice? What exactly makes signals 'separately identifiable' versus 'unique'?

questions.title: What constitutes a 'clear and unambiguous' disavowal of claim scope during prosecution?
questions.question_body: Finesse Wireless originally claimed 'digitally multiplying two or three signals' but amended to 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' to overcome prior art. AT&T argued this surrendered claim scope over two-signal products, but the Federal Circuit held there was no 'clear and unambiguous' disavowal under Continental Circuits v. Intel. I'm confused about where the line is drawn. If changing 'two or three' to just 'three' isn't a clear disavowal of two-signal products, what would be? How explicit does the prosecution history need to be?

questions.title: Why didn't the waiver of the 'unique signals' argument preclude appellate review?
questions.question_body: The district court found that AT&T waived its argument that 'three signals' must be unique by not raising it at the Rule 50(a) stage. But the Federal Circuit still analyzed the merits of whether the accused radios use three signals and perform seven multiplications. Did the appellate court implicitly reject the waiver finding, or is there some exception that allows arguments to be raised for the first time on appeal? I thought Rule 50(b) motions were strictly limited to arguments made in Rule 50(a) motions.

questions.title: How specifically must an expert map accused product features to claim limitations?
questions.question_body: For the '775 patent, the expert identified three multiplications from a Nokia document but never explained how they mapped to the seven multiplications claimed. Finesse tried to provide a mapping on appeal, but the court said this evidence was never presented to the jury. What level of mapping detail is actually required? Does an expert have to walk through each claim limitation element-by-element, or is it enough to identify generally corresponding features? At what point does the gap between evidence and claim elements become legally fatal?

questions.title: Why vacate damages rather than remand for a new trial?
questions.question_body: The Federal Circuit reversed JMOL on noninfringement and simply 'vacated' the damages award. Since the infringement verdict is gone, what happens to the damages? Does 'vacated' mean the damages issue is moot, or does it leave open the possibility of a new damages trial if there's a new infringement finding on remand? And why didn't the court need to address the defendants' alternative argument for a new trial on damages?
